state_changing_checks.rationale: Scheme, host and port must match an allowlist entry exactly. Origin is a header and a request that is not from a browser can set it to anything, which is why it is not sufficient alone against a native attacker.

The csrfToken scheme in packages/schemas/openapi-v1.yaml, carried in X-VibeMaxxing-CSRF and compared against the value stored with the session. It is the only one of the three an attacker cannot produce without already reading a response from the allowlisted origin.

ADR-015 sets SameSite=Lax on the session cookie, which stops a cross-site POST before the request is dispatched. It carries no reason code because a browser that enforces it produces no server response.

bearer_exemption.rationale: A cross-site request cannot attach a bearer credential the attacking page does not hold, so cross-site request forgery does not apply. Native client requests are exempt from these two checks and from nothing else; the native client is not a browser and has no origin at all.

loopback_controls.title: Host header allowlist
loopback_controls.closes: DNS rebinding. A rebound request still carries Host: evil.example because the browser sends the name it was given and not the address it resolved to, so a server that checks Host cannot be rebound and a server that ignores it cannot tell the two apart.

loopback_controls.title: Origin header rules for state-changing requests
loopback_controls.closes: A web page talking to the daemon. Absent is permitted because the native shell and CLI are not browsers and send no origin; any other value means a page is on the other end.

loopback_controls.title: No credentials in a browser-reachable form
loopback_controls.closes: Forgery that survives the first two controls. A cookie is attached automatically by the browser to a forged cross-site request; a header is not.

loopback_controls.title: A random high port recorded in the local state directory
loopback_controls.closes: Targeting without probing. A fixed well-known port is the single fact an attacking page needs; a random port makes it enumerate roughly sixteen thousand possibilities.

loopback_controls.title: Bind verification before listening
loopback_controls.closes: A configuration path that exposes the listener on a routable interface. The listener resolves its configured bind address and refuses to start if the result is not a loopback address.

loopback_controls.title: No CORS headers, ever
loopback_controls.closes: A cross-origin consumer acquiring read access by configuration. There is no legitimate cross-origin consumer of a local control API, so a preflight receives 403 rather than an allow.

loopback_controls.title: Idle and absolute token expiry
loopback_controls.closes: A token left in a browser tab's memory remaining useful indefinitely.

loopback_controls.title: Local rate limit
loopback_controls.closes: Port enumeration by a probing page. At ten attempts a minute, enumerating a sixteen-thousand-port range takes over a day, by which time the daemon has restarted onto a different port.

controls.note: Checked before routing, so a rebound request never reaches a handler.
The session token is delivered as a URL fragment when the shell opens the dashboard, held in memory by the page, and sent in a request header. It is never stored in a cookie.
The idle figure matches challenge_expiry_seconds, the existing repository figure for a short-lived local credential. Closing the dashboard revokes the token immediately.

loopback_listeners.residual_exposure: An unauthenticated localhost endpoint that any local process can POST at. The controls here stop a web page from reaching it; they do not stop a local process, and no loopback control can, because a local process running as the participant is indistinguishable from the participant. Any process able to reach the socket can mint token counts. The origin controls are therefore never a substitute for treating every received datapoint as untrusted input, and no evidence ceiling above private-analytics may be claimed on the strength of them.

controls.note: Stricter than the dashboard because no browser is ever a legitimate OTLP exporter. The exporter is the local agent process and sends no Origin.
The receiver holds no credential to keep out of a cookie. Recorded as not-applicable rather than omitted, because an absent key would read as a control nobody considered.
The exporter reads the port from the same local state file the daemon writes, so a random port costs the legitimate exporter nothing.
ADAPTER_ONE_CLAUDE_CODE_OTEL.md already required this for the receiver; it is restated here because it applies to every loopback listener.
There is no session token to expire. The receiver is unauthenticated by design under D-100, so this control has nothing to bind to.

Every request to this listener is unauthenticated by construction, so the probe limit is the whole limit and it bounds legitimate export as well as probing. A 60-second exporter interval fits inside it and a burst does not. The tension is recorded rather than resolved: raising the figure for this listener needs its own decision, because the same number is what makes port enumeration take a day.

loopback_refusal_codes.description: The request's Host was not exactly a loopback authority on the listener's port. Refused before routing. This is the DNS-rebinding refusal.
A state-changing request carried an Origin that was neither absent nor an exact loopback origin on the listener's port, which means a web page is talking to the daemon.
A CORS preflight reached a loopback listener. It is answered 403 with no Access-Control-* header rather than with an allow.
The dashboard session token passed its 900-second idle window or its 3600-second absolute lifetime, or the dashboard was closed and the token revoked.
The local rate limit was exceeded: 60 requests per minute against a valid token, 10 per minute for a request carrying none.
